input: Feedback control is one of the most fundamental concepts in process engineering, and a temperature loop on a process vessel provides an excellent illustration of how it works in practice. The purpose of the loop is to hold the temperature of the vessel at a desired set point by adjusting the flow of the stream that heats or cools it. The first element in the loop is the sensor, which measures the temperature inside the vessel and converts that measurement into a signal that can be transmitted to the controller. The controller then compares the measured temperature with the set point and calculates the correction required in order to reduce the error between them. The final element, typically a control valve on the heating stream, receives the signal from the controller and moves in response, thereby changing the flow that performs the heating or cooling. Finally, the process itself closes the loop, since the altered flow changes the very temperature that the sensor measures. Crucially, the sign of the feedback in such a loop is negative, and this is precisely what makes the arrangement self-correcting: a temperature above the set point leads to a reduction in heating, while a temperature below the set point leads to an increase, so that every deviation generates a response opposing it. With the opposite sign, by contrast, the same equipment would drive the temperature progressively further away from the set point, which underscores why the sign of the feedback is such an important aspect of the loop.
target:
A feedback control loop holds the temperature of a process vessel at its set point by acting on the stream that heats or cools the vessel. The loop has four parts, taken in the order the signal travels. The sensor measures the vessel temperature and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can read. The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point and calculates the correction the error calls for. The final element receives the signal from the controller and moves the flow that does the heating or cooling, most often a valve on the heating stream. The process itself completes the loop, because the new flow changes the temperature the sensor measures.

The sign of the feedback is negative, and the sign is what makes the loop a regulator rather than an amplifier. A temperature above the set point produces a correction that reduces the heating, and a temperature below the set point produces a correction that increases it, so each deviation generates its own counteraction. With the opposite sign, the same hardware would drive the temperature away from the set point at every step. The loop also corrects disturbances it never measures directly, such as a colder feed, because their effect arrives at the sensor as a temperature error and is answered there. What the loop cannot do is hold the temperature exactly at the set point while a disturbance persists: a sustained correction requires a sustained error to drive it, and the size of that offset is a property of the controller, whose settings this passage does not take up.
